title: Data is the material: Project 1 opens, and my first p5.js sketch
introduction:
Two sessions this week. On Tuesday Boyd opened the new unit, communication technologies, and with it Project 1. Project 0 was a broadcast: I had a story and an aesthetic and you came to experience it. Project 1 is a duet: two websites that use each other's live data, so the meaning grows out of the conversation between them.

On Wednesday we had the first p5.js workshop with Ross. I had used p5 before in Ideas in Art & Tech (the running stickman and the flock), but always starting from someone else's code. This time I started from an empty editor and built a small solar system: a sun, two planets, a moon, two orbit lines, 150 twinkling stars and a comet with a tail.

This post covers Tuesday and Wednesday. I will add Thursday's Project 1 workshop and Friday's session later this week.
related_work:
Boyd's lecture was about data as the material of the web. An architect decides where the wall goes, but the material is brick and glass; for a website the material is data: text, images, sound, video, tables, 3D, code. For every file you ask two questions: can the browser read it, and how heavy is it? If the browser cannot decode it, the data might as well not exist. Encoding is the rule that maps characters to numbers (UTF-8 for the web), and when the rule is read wrongly you get broken characters, which is exactly what happened to some people's GitHub uploads. A raster image writes down every pixel, so it is heavy; a vector image is an instruction, 'draw a blue circle here', so it is light. p5.js draws with vectors. Compression means losing information on purpose: a JPEG says 'all of this is blue' and drops the small differences that nobody can see.

Then he moved from making content to sending it. Hole in Space (1980) put a screen and a camera on a street in New York and another in Los Angeles, so people in the two cities could see and talk to each other live, long before video calls existed [1]. Nothing on the internet travels whole: it is cut into packets that can arrive late, out of order or not at all. TCP asks and confirms every packet; UDP just shouts 'next' and accepts losses, which is why a video call stutters instead of stopping. A WebSocket keeps one line open, and a server in the middle passes data from site 1 to site 2. That server-in-the-middle is what Project 1 is built on [2]. Boyd showed his own demo: two people drive one car, a camera tracks each face and moves a head made of PNG parts. No video is sent, only where things should be, so it is light and fast.

Ross said something about learning that I want to keep. Look at the official tutorials and the Examples page, copy a bit, change a bit, and it becomes yours; that is a normal part of learning. On AI he was clear: you need some knowledge yourself to learn critically from AI, because if all you do is copy and paste code you will not learn [3].
method:
We started together: createCanvas, background, circle, fill, then the built-in variables mouseX, mouseY and frameCount, then an if on mouseIsPressed to change the colour. After that it was free practice and Ross walked around.

My order was: a yellow sun in the middle; a planet whose position is sunX + cos(frameCount * 0.02) * 150 for x and the same with sin for y; a second planet, slower and further out (0.008, 230); a moon that uses the same formula but with the first planet as its centre; two orbit lines with noFill and a white stroke; 150 stars in a for loop, with randomSeed so they stay in place and a sin on the alpha so they twinkle; and a comet made of 12 circles that get smaller and fainter, whose position comes from frameCount % 1000 so it flies out and comes back. At the end I changed the canvas to 800 x 800 and moved the sun's position into three variables at the top, sunX, sunY and speed, so one change moves everything. The sketch is online [4]; the three p5 pages I leaned on were Sine and Cosine, Repeating with Loops and Variables and Change [5][6][7].
results_discussion:
Most of the afternoon was errors, and the errors taught more than the working lines.

I wrote background(RGB(2, 1, 1)) and p5 told me RGB is not a function: the three numbers go straight in. I wrote fill(red) without quotes and the circle stayed black, because red without quotes is a variable that does not exist. I typed fremecount and got an error, because p5 names are lower case then capitals, and one wrong letter is a different name. I closed the if and the else but forgot the closing brace of draw, and got 'Unexpected end of input': every opening brace needs a closing one. I pasted the planet code outside draw and got 'fill is not defined', because the drawing functions only work inside setup or draw.

The two mistakes that taught me the most were about the orbit. First, the x line used 0.02 and the y line used 0.03, so the planet did not go round in a circle but drew a strange path. Both lines must share the same speed and the same radius. Second, my orbit line used 300 for the width and 180 for the height, so it was an ellipse and the planet never sat on it. The orbit line's diameter must be the radius times two: my planet at radius 230 needed a circle of 460. That also settled a question from the class. Ross said the third number of circle is the radius; the documentation says diameter, and the orbit line proved it.

What I understand now: draw runs sixty times a second, frameCount is the clock, and everything that moves is frameCount times a speed, passed through cos and sin to turn a growing number into a position on a circle. When Ross came past he asked how I got the comet to have a trail, and said it looked cool. That was the only line of the day I did not expect to write.

I asked AI when I was stuck (why the circle was black, how the orbit radius relates to the line), but I typed every line in the editor myself and broke it and fixed it until I knew why it worked, which is the way Ross described.

The lecture also fits my Project 1 idea. Two people each pick an emotion; each sees the other person's childhood silhouette in that emotion; after a few rounds they see the full picture. Only a few bytes travel, which emotion was chosen, not images, exactly like Boyd's car demo where the face stays on the local machine and only positions are sent. p5 will draw it, a WebSocket will carry it.
conclusion_future_work: Reading for the week is the first chapters of Flusser, Into the Universe of Technical Images [8]. Thursday is the Project 1 workshop and Friday the technical session; I will add both to this post. At the weekend I start coding the Project 1 logic. One decision from today: my Ideas in Art & Tech planet piece in week 8 will not be made in p5, because three of my pieces are already p5 and I want a different kind of making.
